conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a brief, 10-question screen that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally since your baby arrived. Everything you share stays confidential between you and your care team, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you this past week. We’ll go one question at a time, and you can answer in your own words. Ready to start?

First question: Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

Hi… okay, I’m ready. 

This past week? Laughing feels pretty hard. My sister sent me a silly meme and I tried to smile, but it just felt forced. Nothing seems that funny right now.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I wish I could say that. Most of the time I feel like I’m just going through the motions. I’ll see or hear something that used to make me giggle, but lately it lands flat—like I’m too tired or heavy inside to really enjoy it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk around the lake, even just binge-watching a show—but now it all feels like another chore. I’ll think “I should want to do that,” but the spark isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that happens a lot. If the baby won’t settle or I can’t get her to nap, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m already failing her. I’ll replay every little thing I did and beat myself up for not knowing better. Rationally I know babies just cry, but the guilt still sits on my chest.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing—what if she spits up and chokes when I’m not looking, what if she stops breathing at night, what if I’m not producing enough milk… I know some worry is normal, but this feels constant, like I can’t turn the volume down.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… it’s like a sudden wave, especially when the house is quiet and she’s finally asleep. My chest gets tight, I can’t catch my breath, and I’m convinced something awful is about to happen—even though I can’t name what. It passes after a few minutes, but those spells leave me shaky and exhausted.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. I’ll look at the pile of laundry or the stack of bottles and feel like I’m drowning. I know it’s just little tasks, but when she’s fussy and I haven’t slept, it feels like I’m carrying bricks on my back. I still get through it, but I’m running on fumes and tears more often than I’d like to admit.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s been happening several nights this week. I’ll finally get her down, but then my mind just keeps spinning—replaying everything I think I messed up, worrying about what tomorrow will bring. I lie there staring at the ceiling, exhausted but unable to drift off. When I do sleep, I wake up at every tiny sound she makes.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… a lot of the time. It’s like there’s this gray cloud hanging over me. I’ll look at her tiny face and feel like I should be glowing, but instead I’m just heavy and weepy. Some mornings I wake up already feeling like I’m failing, and the sadness sticks around for most of the day.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

A few times this week. Usually it’s when I can’t get her to stop crying or when I realize I haven’t eaten a real meal all day. I’ll just sit on the couch with tears rolling down, feeling like I’m drowning, even though I can’t always explain exactly why.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I might feel overwhelmed and cry, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like me again and be a good mom to her.

You've shared that the past week has felt heavy-laughter and joy seem out of reach, daily tasks feel like climbing a mountain with bricks on your back, and waves of worry or panic catch you off guard even when your baby is safe. You cry easily, blame yourself when your daughter fusses, and lie awake running through fears, yet you continue to show up for her with deep love and no thoughts of harming yourself.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes complete loss of ability to laugh, indicating anhedonia and emotional numbness</sym>, <sym>Patient reports total loss of anticipatory joy, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intense self-blame that feels overwhelming and persistent, matching "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, pervasive, uncontrollable worries about infant safety despite awareness they may be excessive, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense panic episodes with physical symptoms (tight chest, breathlessness) and catastrophic thoughts, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>She reports frequent overwhelm and difficulty coping, but still manages to complete tasks, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption due to distressing thoughts, matching "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness with imagery of a “gray cloud,” weepiness, and waking up already feeling low—aligned with “Yes, most of the time.”</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying episodes multiple times in the past week, explicitly linked to overwhelming infant care and self-neglect, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Your score of 25 places you well above the threshold (≥14) indicating probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset; you endorse core symptoms daily for most of the past week: <sym>depressed mood</sym>, <sym>markedly diminished interest</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>feelings of worthlessness</sym>, <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, and <sym>anxiety</sym>. These map onto <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. You denied self-harm, reducing immediate safety risk, but severity warrants urgent assessment and support. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Discuss evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, peer support groups, and consider antidepressant options compatible with breastfeeding
3. Plan daily 15-minute rest periods; accept help with housework and night feeds to protect sleep
4. Use brief grounding techniques during panic: slow breathing, naming five objects you see, sipping cold water
5. Schedule follow-up EPDS in two weeks to track progress
6. Crisis line numbers in phone for nights when worries spike: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline or Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – 2–3 wk post-delivery

Symptom profile  
• Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia (Q1, Q2, Q8, Q9)  
• Marked guilt / self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)  
• Daily, distressing anxiety/panic without clear trigger (Q4, Q5)  
• Overwhelm and sense of “drowning” in routine tasks (Q6)  
• Mood-congruent insomnia (unable to fall or stay asleep despite exhaustion) (Q7)

Patterns  
Symptoms present most days, interfere with functioning, but no self-harm ideation endorsed (Q10).

Screening significance  
High endorsement consistent with probable major depressive episode with anxious features, postpartum onset; also meets clinical threshold for postpartum anxiety. No current safety concerns (denies SI/HI).

Next step  
Recommend prompt formal evaluation (diagnostic interview plus EPDS scoring) and discussion of support / treatment options.
